claims.text: A direct W–CuCrZr interface suffers from thermal expansion mismatch.
A direct W–CuCrZr interface has suboptimal interfacial bonding.
Thermal expansion mismatch and suboptimal bonding at a direct W–CuCrZr interface produce high residual stresses.
High residual stresses at a direct W–CuCrZr interface cause early interfacial degradation under reactor-relevant conditions.
A thin Mo interlayer between W and CuCrZr improves interfacial bonding.
A thin Mo interlayer between W and CuCrZr reduces residual stresses under extreme thermal cycling.
The Mo interlayer acts as a buffer that accommodates the difference in thermal expansion coefficients between W and CuCrZr.
The Mo interlayer provides a diffusion barrier at the W–CuCrZr interface.
The diffusion-barrier behavior of the Mo interlayer enhances interfacial adhesion.
Mo has a coefficient of thermal expansion intermediate between those of W and CuCrZr.
Mo has a high melting point suitable for the proposed high-temperature application.
The Mo interlayer creates a more gradual thermomechanical transition between W and CuCrZr.
A more gradual transition through Mo lowers interfacial residual stresses during cyclic thermal loading.
W/Mo/CuCrZr joints will have greater interfacial strength than direct W/CuCrZr joints.
W/Mo/CuCrZr joints will resist thermal-cycling-induced degradation better than direct W/CuCrZr joints.
The benefit of the Mo interlayer may diminish outside the standard fusion-reactor operating temperature or thermal-cycle-frequency range.
The benefit of the Mo interlayer depends on controlling its thickness.
